messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Censored logistic ordinal regression
parts:
Hi,

I would like to estimate a regression model for an ordinal dependent variable that is censored in the following way,

score = ifelse(rank <= 10, 
                     rank,
                     11 or any other value I choose)

Specifically this is for data where I have a competition where participants either rank in the top 10 or they do not.

I was thinking about using an ordinal logistic regression to estimate this model but at the moment am not sure whether this is possible. I presume I would need a lccdf function to do this, but not sure one exists in Stan?

Any other ideas?

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Re: Censored logistic ordinal regression
parts:
One approach I can think of would be to do a sort of two step model, where in the first step we determine whether the rank is in the top 10, then if so, continue onto a second stage where we determine the rank. A bit like a zero-inflated poisson or something similar...

However thoughts still welcome here! Not sure the above is exactly what I want because I really just want one set of parameters rather than two (one for the binomial first stage, the other for ordinal regression in the second).

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Censored logistic ordinal regression
parts:
The top 10 sounds arbitrary here. So rather than trying
to build it into the model, I'd build a model ranking
people in the competition then deal with the top ten
as a posterior predictive quantity. Such as the probabilty
that a participant is in the top 10.

- Bob

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Censored logistic ordinal regression
parts:
You could use a [0,1] parameter, let it theta and map your ranking 1-10 by theta * ordinal and (1-theta) is the rest.
But I would not do it. Instead I would define the "performance" and later do a mapping to the ranking. 
Which is what I read in Bob's comment.

Andre

Exactly.

It's like modeling two team's scores, then seeing who'll win rather
than modeling the win/loss directly.

That's how something like the Bradley-Terry model works (which works
out to be the proper stats for modeling something like ELO and it's
used in many college rankings).

- Bob
